title: AI may soon change what it means to be a theoretical physicist
gist: Frontier AI models now perform most well-defined theoretical-physics calculations: GPT-6 Astra solved 49 of 50 unpublished expert problems in Suvrat Raju's TheoPhysEval for under $3 each, saturating the benchmark before release. AI agents are driving a ~30% surge in hep-th arXiv submissions and threatening the training path for young physicists, while the real bottleneck for questions like quantum gravity remains experimental testability; physicists guess physics trails math by 6–12 months.

insights.claim: Suvrat Raju's TheoPhysEval benchmark used unpublished problems that take top theoretical physicists about a day each, specifically to avoid LLM memorization of answers found online.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Private, never-published problem sets are the credible way to measure frontier model reasoning versus memorization.
insights.locator: LLMs have been trained on the whole Internet

insights.claim: Leading AI models solved about 60 percent of TheoPhysEval problems in preliminary September results, and by completion GPT-6 Astra solved 49 of 50 correctly, also identifying subtle errors in the human-written answers.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Rapid capability jumps within months show expert-level scientific calculation is now commoditizing — bullish for frontier labs' scientific-use revenue.
insights.quote: Astra argued that it hadn’t made a mistake—the humans had
insights.locator: Curious to know where Astra was struggling

insights.claim: Each correct GPT-6 Astra answer on TheoPhysEval cost less than $3 of compute on average and came from a single human prompt.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Expert-day-equivalent work for <$3 implies massive cost deflation for research labor.
insights.quote: less than the price of coffee in Paris
insights.locator: Each correct answer had cost less than $3

insights.claim: Raju will not build a second version of TheoPhysEval because AI has hit the ceiling of well-defined calculations humans can pose, leaving only open research, which is not an evaluation.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Benchmarks for frontier science are running out; future capability signals will come from real discoveries, not evals.
insights.quote: We’ve kind of hit the ceiling of well-defined calculations that people can do.
insights.locator: People gave us the hardest problems they could

insights.claim: A Turkish physicist reported that Claude Opus 5.5 recreated the core of his PhD thesis in 10 hours, work that took him a year and 500 pages of hand calculations.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Orders-of-magnitude speedups on technical work underpin demand for frontier model tokens in academia.
insights.locator: In October, a Turkish physicist posted on X

insights.claim: Ed Witten credits Opus in recent papers, and Juan Maldacena acknowledged OpenAI models on two papers this year, using them for calculations and literature search.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Adoption by the field's most eminent figures legitimizes AI-assisted science and accelerates mainstream uptake.
insights.quote: calculations that in the past were maybe too long.
insights.locator: Ed Witten, the most-cited living theorist

insights.claim: UT Austin physicist Andreas Karch runs AI agents around the clock and uses GPT-6 Astra to audit one old paper a day, finding issues in nearly every one.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: AI error-checking of the existing literature is an emergent use case that could reshape peer review.
insights.quote: Pretty much every paper that I send it, it has something to say.
insights.locator: Karch ruefully admitted

insights.claim: OpenAI gives physicist Andreas Karch a free high-tier ChatGPT subscription, and Anthropic gave Harvard's Matthew Schwartz free tokens, with contracts with a number of academics, as frontier labs court physicists.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Labs are subsidizing elite academic usage as marketing and capability showcase — a customer-acquisition cost in the race for science credibility.
insights.quote: And now I’m seeing what you can do with tokenmaxxing.
insights.locator: Schwartz isn’t paying for all of those tokens

insights.claim: Harvard's Matthew Schwartz ran about 20 concurrent AI sessions, each working a different problem with 10 to 20 agents per thread.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Single researchers consuming hundreds of parallel agents signal very high token-demand elasticity in research.
insights.locator: Harvard’s Matthew Schwartz uses AI agents even more aggressively

insights.claim: MIT's Daniel Harlow says in his area most work is figuring out what to do, so by the time he has a calculation he is 95% done, making LLMs helpful for learning adjacent fields but not a category change.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: AI value in science is concentrated in computation-heavy subfields; conceptual work remains less automated for now.
insights.quote: the vast majority of the work is figuring out what to do.
insights.locator: Of course, this isn’t the whole story

insights.claim: From January to October, submissions to arXiv's hep-th (high-energy physics theory) category rose about 30 percent year over year, versus a maximum annual jump of 8 percent over the prior two decades.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A quantifiable AI productivity signal in research output — a proxy to track AI's diffusion into science.
insights.locator: A flood of papers

insights.claim: Matthew Schwartz describes many AI-era physics papers as poorly written but scientifically probably solid, while Scott Aaronson notes nobody has time to read them all.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Filtering/curation, not generation, becomes the scarce resource — opportunity for AI-driven review and discovery tools.
insights.quote: It’s like this endless buffet. Even if it’s the most amazing food, how much of it can you digest?
insights.locator: But nobody knows for sure because nobody has time

insights.claim: Syracuse physicist Aron Wall expects the paper flood to increase reliance on personal references and relationships to find relevant work.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Information overload strengthens network-based gatekeeping in science.
insights.locator: Eventually, and perhaps soon, the endless buffet

insights.claim: No major AI-aided physics discovery is yet visible in the paper flood; the closest is OpenAI's October announcement that a model proved pure Yang-Mills holds together in four dimensions, a 1,147-page Lean proof verified by a panel and half of a Millennium Prize problem.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Formal-verified mathematical breakthroughs are a credibility milestone for OpenAI's scientific claims.
insights.locator: Physics might be just months behind mathematics

insights.claim: Many physicists view the AI Yang-Mills proof as technically impressive but confirming something everybody already believed, rather than new physics.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Temper hype: marquee AI results may lack scientific novelty even when formally impressive.
insights.locator: But the consensus among physicists seems to be

insights.claim: Scott Aaronson argues AI came for math and programming first because they have self-contained ways to verify answers, which powers AI training, and physicists he knows guess physics is six to 12 months behind math.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Domains with cheap automatic verification are next for AI disruption — useful heuristic for which professions/sectors get automated first.
insights.quote: we have very, very self-contained ways to verify whether an answer is right or not
insights.locator: Aaronson told me some of the physicists he knows

insights.claim: One of 722 math papers OpenAI released on October 6 appears to show that if a cousin of the P versus NP conjecture were false, testing the black hole firewall paradox would become more feasible, weakening Harlow's defense.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: AI-generated math is starting to touch foundational physics questions.
insights.locator: But as Aaronson pointed out to me

insights.claim: Matthew Schwartz predicts AI will do most creative physics steps and write papers end to end by next summer, and that a year later humans won't understand what it is doing.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Aggressive insider timelines for autonomous AI science — if right, research labor markets shift within ~2 years.
insights.quote: It’s certain by next summer, the AI will be able to do most of those creative steps on its own and really do papers end to end.
insights.locator: But Schwartz expects this situation to be temporary

insights.claim: Prominent OpenAI researcher roon speculated publicly about a unified field theory or quantum gravity within the next 12 months.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: AI-industry insiders signal very bullish expectations for scientific breakthroughs — a hype indicator to watch.
insights.quote: unified field theory / quantum gravity within the next 12 months?
insights.locator: AI industry insiders seem to think the same

insights.claim: Directly observing quantum gravity effects would require a collider roughly a quadrillion times more powerful than the Large Hadron Collider, so even an AI-generated quantum gravity theory would likely remain untestable.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: AI can't shortcut physical validation — experimental infrastructure, not ideas, constrains fundamental physics progress.
insights.quote: the problem isn’t the ideas, it’s the experiments.
insights.locator: The Large Hadron Collider is the most powerful particle accelerator

insights.claim: If progress depends on burning large amounts of compute, theoretical physics may become collective like experimental physics, pooling resources and jointly applying for grants, as proposed recently by 51 physicists.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Compute could become a major line item in science funding, creating a new institutional customer for AI labs and cloud providers.
insights.locator: If it doesn’t hold, one possibility

insights.claim: Many physicists expect AI to shift theoretical physics from calculation toward conceptual thought experiments, with Raju saying AI may free them from 'shut up and calculate'.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Human comparative advantage moves to problem framing and conceptual work.
insights.quote: [Maybe AI] frees us up to stop and think, and it lets us think about ambitious problems that we couldn’t think of earlier,
insights.locator: The end of “shut up and calculate”

insights.claim: Physicists warn that AI removing routine calculation eliminates the traditional way students build reputation and intuition, and Raju is not taking new PhD students until their prospects are clearer.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Early-career pipeline disruption in elite STEM is an early indicator for AI's effect on entry-level knowledge work.
insights.quote: It’s not clear how you jump over that step
insights.locator: An uncertain future for young physicists

insights.claim: Physicists fear being scooped because others can feed a shared idea to AI agents to solve, making researchers more guarded about big ideas.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: AI may reduce open collaboration in science, slowing informal knowledge sharing.
insights.quote: If you tell somebody, they’re going to run and ask the agent to solve it,
insights.locator: Karch also mentioned a burgeoning fear of getting scooped

insights.claim: Trump administration science funding cuts compound physicists' career risks, frontier labs aren't hiring many physicists outside top departments, and some students write training problems for Mercor or Scale AI at $80 to $100 an hour.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Data-labeling firms are tapping a growing pool of displaced PhD-level talent for expert training data.
insights.quote: This is good money on the side, but it’s not a career,
insights.locator: All this is compounded by funding cuts

insights.claim: Matthew Schwartz and Juan Maldacena say they would accept AI generating fundamental physics knowledge as long as it can be understood, while Daniel Harlow says he would refuse and not even read the result.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Leading scientists are split on AI-driven discovery, foreshadowing cultural resistance in research institutions.
insights.quote: I think it doesn’t matter who generates the knowledge,
insights.locator: The trade

insights.claim: If AI generates physics discoveries humans cannot produce, theoretical physicists may become interpreters of knowledge rather than discoverers, resembling a humanities field — a state math may already be entering.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Long-run shift in the value of human expertise from discovery to translation and teaching.
